Echoes of the Present: 1979 Honda Accord 4-Door Archive Road Test

By Marco Rossi Senior Supercar & Aerodynamics Editor • via Car and Driver Wire

Source & Photography: Car and Driver Wire Dispatch Verified Editorial Asset
⚡ Executive Takeaways & Key Highlights

⚡ EDITORIAL TAKE • MARCO ROSSI Senior Supercar & Aerodynamics Editor

The Benchmark for Track-Tolerant Engineering

In the high-stakes supercar arena, pure horsepower is no longer enough to claim supremacy. This dispatch from Car and Driver emphasizes how cutting-edge downforce balance, electronic limited-slip differentials, and hybrid torque-vectoring are reshaping driver engagement. Exotic marques must prove that extreme performance can harmonize with reliability, thermal endurance, and road compliance.

Big Picture: Lap times at benchmark proving grounds and early client allocations will reveal whether this performance envelope disrupts the existing supercar hierarchy.

Japanese manufacturers are building the best small American cars money can buy. Firms like Datsun and Subaru cling to products that are more in the Japa­nese tradition, but Toyota, Mazda, Mit­subishi, and Honda are cranking out trick little cars that would warm the cockles of a Detroit product planner’s heart. Of these, Honda’s Accord is the best. It is also, alas, the most expensive, but it is a class act and a car that could probably solve the transportation prob­lems of at least 75 percent of the people currently driving around on the high­ways of the good old U.S. of A.

📌 The Core Development

The great trading companies of Japan have apparently decided that the world wants cars combining the size and weight of European econoboxes with the cushy velour and gadget features of traditional American bargain-cruisers, and the sales of Japanese cars in the Western world would seem to support them in that point of view.
